articles.title: Conadis lanza grave advertencia: gobiernos regionales y municipios desvían recursos destinados para atender a personas con discapacidad
articles.summary: Presidenta del Conadis, Olga Villalobos, indicó que los gobiernos locales y regionales “le están sacando la vuelta” a la ley, ya que destina el presupuesto para atender a personas con discapacidad a otras áreas o implementan oficinas sin brindar ningún servicio
articles.body_text: El 16 de octubre se conmemora en el país el Día Nacional de la Persona con Discapacidad, por lo que El Comercio entrevistó a Olga Mercedes Villalobos, presidenta del Consejo Nacional para la Integración de la Persona con Discapacidad (Conadis), para conocer los objetivos de su gestión y los retos que afronta un ciudadano con discapacidad en el país. Un punto saltante de la entrevista es que, según Villalobos, los gobiernos regionales y las municipalidades reportan que destinan recursos para supuestamente atender a las personas con discapacidad, pero remarcó que se ha comprobado que existen oficinas que no ofrecen ningún tipo de servicio o el presupuesto se destina a otras áreas. 1. ¿Cuál es el rol de Conadis frente a una persona con discapacidad? El rol del Conadis es promover y garantizar el reconocimiento y ejercicio de los derechos de las personas con discapacidad, impulsando políticas públicas, articulando acciones con las entidades del Estado en sus tres niveles de gobierno y supervisando el cumplimiento de las obligaciones fiscalizables. Asimismo, brinda orientación a las personas con discapacidad y sus familias, promueve la eliminación de barreras que limitan su participación en la sociedad y contribuye a generar las condiciones necesarias para que puedan ejercer sus derechos en igualdad de condiciones con las demás personas. 2. ¿Cuáles son los objetivos de su gestión? Soy una educadora especialista en discapacidad y lo más importante en este momento es el tema de la educación inclusiva, ya que, sin ella, una persona con discapacidad no podrá tener oportunidades a nivel de estudios técnicos productivos y a nivel universitario, por tanto, seguirá estando en un círculo de pobreza. 3. ¿Qué retos afronta una persona con discapacidad en el Perú? En el Perú, las personas con discapacidad enfrentan múltiples barreras que dificultan el ejercicio pleno de sus derechos y su participación en igualdad de condiciones en la sociedad. Entre los principales retos se encuentran persistencia de prejuicios, estereotipos y prácticas discriminatorias, así como barreras de accesibilidad en los espacios públicos, el transporte público, la información y las comunicaciones. También enfrenta dificultades para acceder a una educación inclusiva, servicios de salud de calidad y oportunidades de empleo digno. A ello se suman las brechas territoriales, especialmente en las zonas rurales, la limitada disponibilidad de servicios de apoyo y las dificultades para ejercer su autonomía. Desde el 2012 no se hace una Enedis (Encuesta Nacional Especializada sobre Discapacidad) y hemos pedidos de manera reiterada al MEF que nos asigne el presupuesto de 16 millones de soles para realizar esta encuesta especializada a través del INEI. Si no se conoce la brecha, es muy difícil generar políticas públicas. Necesitamos saber dónde está la persona con discapacidad, qué discapacidad tiene y cuál es su necesidad. 4. ¿Cómo ha venido evolucionando el tema de los derechos para las personas con discapacidad en las últimas décadas? Nuestra legislación ha experimentado importantes cambios en la manera de comprender la discapacidad, transitando del modelo médico-rehabilitador al modelo social y de derechos humanos, que reconoce la importancia de eliminar las barreras del entorno. 5. ¿A cuántas personas con discapacidad el Conadis brinda asistencia o cuántas personas tiene registradas? A través del Registro Nacional de la Persona con Discapacidad, el Conadis cuenta, al 15 de octubre de 2026, con 631 330 inscripciones. Asimismo, mediante la Red Alivia Perú, uno de nuestros principales servicios de orientación y acompañamiento, hemos atendido a 26,720 personas en lo que va del año, facilitándoles el acceso a información, servicios públicos y el ejercicio de derechos de las personas con discapacidad y sus familias. 6. ¿Conadis realiza visitas inopinadas para garantizar servicios de calidad a personas con discapacidad? Conadis ejerce su competencia de fiscalización y sanción a través de la Dirección de Fiscalización y Sanciones. Anualmente aprueba un Plan de Fiscalizaciones y estas se desarrollan de acuerdo con un programa establecido. Durante el año 2026, se realizaron 527 fiscalización a nivel nacional. De este total, 313 corresponden a fiscalizaciones ordinarias, cuyo objetivo es verificar el cumplimiento de la normativa y, de detectarse incumplimientos, pueden dar lugar al inicio de un procedimiento administrativo sancionador; y 214 corresponden a fiscalizaciones orientativas, de carácter preventivo. A diferencia de las ordinarias, estas acciones no tienen como finalidad imponer sanciones, sino brindar recomendaciones y asistencia técnica para que las entidades adecuen su actuación a la normativa vigente. Asimismo, estamos efectuando supervisiones a las Omaped para verificar su implementación y prestación de servicios a las personas con discapacidad. Se han visitado más de 40 OMAPED en Lima. 7. ¿Qué expectativas tiene respecto al anuncio de la presidenta Keiko Fujimori de que el próximo año se ampliará el presupuesto del programa social Contigo a fin de incorporar a más de 100,000 personas con discapacidad? En realidad, es un hecho histórico que ha logrado la gestión de la presidenta Keiko Fujimori en articulación con nuestra ministra de la Mujer y Poblaciones Vulnerables, María Seminario. Desde el año 2024 solo eran beneficiarios 142,771 y la proyección del presupuesto para el 2027 no estaba contemplado un aumento, situación que como Conadis nos preocupaba porque había en lista de espera un promedio de 116,200 personas. En las anteriores gestiones de gobierno no se tuvo la prioridad de ampliar la atención de la pensión, que es de 300 soles bimensuales a las personas con discapacidad. Los requisitos para acceder a la pensión son: ser una persona con discapacidad severa y estar en situación de pobreza. 8. ¿Se cumple la norma que establece que las entidades públicas deben contratar un mínimo de 5% de su personal con personas con discapacidad, mientras que, en el sector privado, las empresas con más de 50 trabajadores deben destinar al menos el 3%? Los resultados obtenidos en las fiscalizaciones realizadas por el Conadis evidencian que solo un ministerio, específicamente el Ministerio de Trabajo y Promoción del Empleo, cumple con la cuota laboral del 5% para las personas con discapacidad. Asimismo, a nivel de gobierno regionales, en las fiscalizaciones realizadas en el año 2025 solo 4 GORE cumplen la cuota: Pasco, Piura, Huánuco y Ucayali. En lo va del 2026, Conadis realizó 82 fiscalizaciones en materia de cumplimiento de la cuota de empleo, y se verificó que 14 entidades cumplieron con la cuota legal del 5%, mientras que 62 entidades no cumplieron con dicha obligación. En los 6 casos restantes, no fue posible determinar el cumplimiento debido a que las entidades administradas no remitieron la información completa requerida para efectuar la evaluación correspondiente. Por otro lado, debemos precisar que, de conformidad con la normativa actual, corresponde al Ministerio de Trabajo, a través de Sunafil, la fiscalización en el ámbito privado. De acuerdo con la información de Sunafil, 245 empresas privadas cumplen con la cuota de empleo para personas con discapacidad en el 2025. 9. ¿Se ha avanzado en el cumplimiento de la norma que dispone que los gobiernos regionales y locales deben destinar el 1% de su presupuesto anual a favor de la población con discapacidad? Mediante la Ley Nº 32139 se estableció que los gobiernos regionales y locales tienen la obligación de contemplar en su presupuesto anual recursos para actividades, que es el 0.5% del Presupuesto Institucional de Apertura para Oredis y Omaped, así como el 0.5% del PIA en inversiones para proyectos y mantenimiento de accesibilidad. El Conadis ha encontrado que, de 24 gobiernos regionales fiscalizados/supervisados, ninguno ha cumplido con asignar el 0.5% de los recursos para financiar actividades y proyectos orientados a la atención de las personas con discapacidad. Asimismo, de 60 gobiernos locales fiscalizados osupervisados, sólo han asignado más del 0.5% de recursos para actividades unos 26 gobiernos locales; mientras que 5 han destinado más del 0.5% para proyectos. El ente rector de fiscalización es la Contraloría. La norma era una esperanza para las personas con discapacidad, ya que se tiene un presupuesto destinado, lo cual en algunos gobiernos regionales es bastante dinero, ya que en determinados casos hay más de 20 millones de soles para destinarlo a la Oficinas Regionales de Atención a las Personas con Discapacidad (Oredis) o a la Oficina Municipal de Atención a la Persona con Discapacidad (Omaped). Sin embargo, ningún GORE ha dado el 1% para temas de discapacidad. Por eso, la persona con discapacidad está tan disconforme y abandonada, ya que hay un presupuesto, pero no se le asigna. Unos cinco gobiernos regionales han cerrado sus Oredis para que ese presupuesto ya no entre a esa oficina y se destine a la Gerencia de Desarrollo Social a fin de distribuirlo a sus diferentes programas sociales. Le han sacado la vuelta a la ley. Hemos quedado con el titular de la PCM, Luis Galarreta, y la ministra de Desarrollo e Inclusión Social, María Seminario, que ni bien se dé las credenciales a las nuevas autoridades municipales y regionales se realizará una inducción sobre la ley que obliga a destinar el 1% para temas de accesibilidad y servicios, ya que tiene una sanción penal. En el caso de Omaped, se ha detectado que en la consulta amigable del MEF se consigna que sí han asignado el 0.5% del presupuesto, sin embargo, cuando se visita el local de Omaped no hay ningún servicio, lo que lleva a preguntarse a dónde se está yendo el dinero.

articles.title: Papa León XIV reaparece en el Ángelus y dice que retomará gradualmente su actividad
articles.summary: Tras reaparecer en el rezo del ángelus en el Vaticano, el papa León XIV agradeció las muestras de apoyo recibidas durante su convalecencia por un adenocarcinoma pulmonar, del que fue operado el pasado martes en Roma
articles.body_text: Tras su alta hospitalaria, el papa León XIV reapareció este domingo en el rezo del Ángelus en el Vaticano, donde explicó que, una vez superada la etapa de su operación pulmonar por un tumor canceroso, retomará sus actividades gradualmente. “Una vez superada esta difícil etapa, como saben, retomaré gradualmente mis actividades, siempre con la ayuda de Dios y sus oraciones”, dijo el pontífice, de 71 años, tras el rezo del Ángelus ante los miles de fieles que se congregaron en la plaza de San Pedro. A las doce del mediodía, León XIV apareció en la ventana de sus aposentos en el Palacio Apostólico vaticano, con buen aspecto, sonriente y saludando a los fieles, que le dedicaron una sonora ovación desde la plaza: “Queridos hermanos y hermanas, ¡buen domingo!, fueron sus primeras palabras antes de comenzar con la plegaria del ángelus. Tras el rezo, el pontífice compartió unas reflexiones, en una alocución más breve de lo que suele ser habitual en estos actos y que aprovechó para dar las gracias a todos los que han orado por él en estos días: “He sentido profundamente su apoyo. ¡Muchas gracias!”. También dedicó su especial gratitud a los médicos, enfermeras y todo el personal del Políclinico Gemelli, donde el pasado martes fue operado de un adenocarcinoma en su pulmón derecho y donde ha estado ingresado hasta ayer sábado, recuperándose de la cirugía. “Esta experiencia me ha acercado especialmente a quienes sufren enfermedades y dolencias”, manifestó Robert Prevost, cuya reaparición en el ángelus duró unos ocho minutos, incluyendo plegaria y alocución posterior. En la plaza de San Pedro, los fieles vivieron con emoción y alegría la reaparición del papa este domingo, según testimonios recabados por EFE: “Pensábamos que no lo íbamos a ver, estamos contentas porque la divina providencia lo permitió”, manifestaron Cindy y Emilia, dos colombianas que expresaron su deseo de que el papa mejore “y lo tengamos muchos años más”. “Tenemos fe en que va a salir todo bien”, decían convencidas Patricia y Rose Esperanza, procedentes de California (EE.UU), para quienes ver hoy a León XIV ha sido “un sueño”. También Ernesto Villegas, sacerdote venezolano, reconocía que el de este domingo ha sido un ángelus de mucha expectación y elogió la fortaleza del pontífice: “El papa ha demostrado es un hombre de armas tomar, no se acobarda, retoma su agenda y sigue adelante como buen pastor que sigue dando la vida por sus ovejas”, dijo a EFE. Hace justo una semana que León XIV, en este mismo rezo, anunció por sorpresa a todo el mundo una inminente operación por la detección de un nódulo en un pulmón. La operación se produjo dos días después, el martes por la tarde, en el hospital Gemelli de Roma: el parte médico posterior informó de la extirpación del lóbulo inferior del pulmón derecho del papa por un adenocarcinoma, un tipo de cáncer. En los días posteriores, León XIV ha tenido una recuperación favorable y, en el momento de su alta, presentaba unas condiciones clínicas “absolutamente satisfactorias”, según Stefano Margaritora, el cirujano que le operó y que dirige la unidad de Cirugía Torácica del Gemelli. La reaparición del papa en el ángelus desde el Vaticano ha despertado expectación también por la posibilidad de que ofreciera detalles sobre su tratamiento o sobre el viaje a Argentina, Uruguay y Perú que está programado del 6 al 17 de noviembre, si bien Robert Prevost no ha hecho referencia a estos temas. Ayer sábado, en una entrevista a medios vaticanos, su cirujano afirmó que el papa puede afrontar esa visita apostólica: “Diría que no hay motivos clínicos por los que no se pueda realizar ese viaje”, manifestó el doctor Margaritora. En esta primera gira latinoamericana del pontificado de León XIV están previstos hasta 14 vuelos, más de cuarenta discursos y reuniones, nueve misas multitudinarias, así como la visita a Cusco, una ciudad situada a más de 3.000 metros sobre el nivel del mar. articles.title: Ica: accidente de tránsito en la antigua Panamericana Sur deja cuatro fallecidos y un herido
articles.summary: Un accidente de tránsito en el kilómetro 230 de la antigua Panamericana Sur, en Pisco, dejó cuatro personas fallecidas, entre ellas un menor de edad, y un herido. La Policía y el Ministerio Público realizan diligencias para esclarecer las circunstancias del siniestro.
articles.body_text: Un accidente de tránsito registrado este sábado en el kilómetro 230 de la antigua carretera Panamericana Sur, en la provincia de Pisco, región Ica, dejó cuatro personas fallecidas, entre ellas un menor de edad, y una herida. Las circunstancias del siniestro son materia de investigación por parte de las autoridades. Integrantes de la Compañía de Bomberos de Pisco acudieron al lugar del accidente y confirmaron el fallecimiento de las cuatro personas. El único sobreviviente, quien resultó herido, fue evacuado de emergencia al Hospital San Juan de Dios de Pisco para recibir atención médica. Tras el siniestro, efectivos de la Policía Nacional del Perú (PNP) acordonaron la zona donde se encontraban los cuerpos para facilitar las diligencias del Ministerio Público. Asimismo, peritos de criminalística llegaron al lugar para recoger evidencias materiales y recabar testimonios de las personas presentes, con el objetivo de esclarecer las causas del accidente. Existe el sistema SAMU de atención médica de urgencia opera durante las 24 horas y es gratuito. Para solicitar su ayuda solo debes marcar el 106. También se cuenta con la Cruz Roja ante desastres naturales u otras crisis que pongan en peligro la salud, seguridad y vida puedes acceder a este servicio humanitario y gratuito llamando al 115.

articles.title: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers and also trying to make on-device, private AI agents a thing.
articles.body_text: Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks. At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell. “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models. Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience. While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity and Salesforce . Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs – companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation. However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs (like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras as well as building their own home-grown chips). So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote. So Nvidia, hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote. Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

articles.title: Apple updates guidelines to ban nudify apps masquerading as regular apps to pass review | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple said that it will ban AI apps that don't moderate offensive content.
articles.body_text: Apple tightened its developer guidelines over the weekend to ban apps that use AI to create offensive content, as well as those that masquerade as regular apps to pass the App Store review process and then turn into nudify apps, or surface those features prominently. The company updated its guidelines with strong language around AI and user-generated content, and how app developers should include enough preventative measures to moderate objectionable or offensive content. “Apps that host user-generated content are required to filter objectionable material, give users a way to report offensive content, and let users block abusive accounts. Apps containing hidden or undocumented features are also prohibited on the App Store, including apps that misrepresent their purpose during review and only reveal harmful capabilities — such as “nudification” — after approval, a tactic commonly known as bait-and-switch,” the company said in a blog post. Apple said that it will remove apps that add features not present in the version submitted for App Store review. The iPhone maker has also updated the language in its legal section to reinforce that it will bar apps promoting human trafficking and exploitation of children. Apple said last year its review process blocked over 150,000 apps from reaching users, and removed 193,000 developer accounts on account of fraud and abuse. In July, San Francisco ordered both Apple and Google to clean up and delete nudification apps from their app stores. City Attorney David Chiu accused the companies of profiting from these apps through store fees. And in April, a Tech Transparency Project report indicated that both tech giants’ stores hosted multiple nudify apps , some of which were rated as suitable for minors. articles.title: Musk pledges to give 'every kid in America' one of his SpaceX shares | TechCrunch
articles.summary: That's more than $10 billion in shares, or around 1% of Musk's current net worth.
articles.body_text: Elon Musk claims he will give one of his SpaceX shares to “every kid in America” in 2027, which would result in a gift worth more than $10 billion based on the current $146 share price of his combination spaceflight and AI company. That’s roughly 1% of his $1 trillion net worth. It’s not clear how Musk plans to do this, though he said in a separate post that he wants to give the shares “directly to the public,” and that this will be the “first of many” shares he’ll donate. President Donald Trump, who Musk spent around $300 million to help elect, has set up bank accounts for children through the Treasury, called Trump Accounts, that can accept stock donations from wealthy donors. Musk did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Musk’s post came just a few hours after Anthropic promised to put 5% of its shares into a new “public benefit fund,” which it intends to use to make “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations” after its upcoming IPO. On Sunday afternoon, Musk replied directly to Anthropic’s post on X about its new fund, suggesting the company should give “directly to the public” instead. “This is what I will be doing,” he wrote in another reply four hours later. Then, overnight, he announced his plans to donate SpaceX stock. There are currently more than 70 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to the Federal Interagency Forum on Child and Family Statistics . Musk owns around 849 million Class A common shares of SpaceX, and more than 5.5 billion Class B supervoting shares. He stands to earn many more. Musk’s philanthropic giving to date has been almost exclusively done through his own Musk Foundation. Despite his negative opinions about philanthropy, it’s the fifth-largest private charitable foundation in the U.S. A recent review by The Economist showed that a majority of the total money laid out by the Musk Foundation over the years has gone to entities tied to Musk in some way. articles.title: Khosla Ventures doubles down on Even Healthcare to challenge India's hospital economics | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Even Healthcare reaches a $300 million valuation in a Khosla Ventures-led round as it plans to expand its hospital network in India.
articles.body_text: Even Healthcare has raised $50 million in a funding round led by Khosla Ventures, as the Indian startup seeks to change how hospitals in the world’s most populous country make money and how doctors are rewarded. The all-equity Series B round also saw participation from Alpha Wave and valued it at $300 million, triple its valuation 18 months ago, according to Even. The latest funding brings Even’s total capital raised to more than $120 million. Hospitals in India typically earn more when patients undergo additional tests, procedures, or longer stays, even when they may not need them. Even wants to change that by focusing on patient care rather than pushing unnecessary treatments that drive up medical bills. That approach has continued to appeal to Khosla Ventures, which has invested in Even since its seed round in 2021. The Silicon Valley venture firm is doubling down as Even moves to build and operate hospitals of its own, giving it greater control over patient care and costs. Vinod Khosla, founder of Khosla Ventures, said Even’s approach goes beyond fixing individual parts of a fragmented healthcare system by bringing financing, technology, and care delivery together. The goal, he said in a prepared statement, is to reward better health outcomes rather than greater use of healthcare services. “The clinical and economic results so far give us conviction that this can become an important new model for healthcare in India and beyond,” Khosla said. Initially, Even relied on partner hospitals to treat its members, but Mayank Banerjee, who founded the startup in 2021 with Matilde Giglio and Alessandro Ialongo, said in an interview that the startup began questioning that model after finding that patients had undergone tests or been recommended surgeries it considered unnecessary. “We think patients are getting not only a bad experience, but insurers are getting a bad economic deal. And as a result, we decided to fix it by building our own hospitals,” Banerjee told TechCrunch. Even has since opened two hospitals in Bengaluru, both of which reached operational profitability, excluding depreciation, within a year of opening, Banerjee stated. The startup plans to open five more hospitals in the southern Indian city over the next six months, funded by its latest round. Banerjee told TechCrunch that Even leases hospital buildings on 20-year agreements and spends on fitting them out and buying medical equipment. Unlike hospitals where doctors may have financial incentives to recommend more procedures, Even pays its doctors fixed salaries — not tying their compensation to the number of tests or surgeries they perform, though Banerjee said doctors can earn bonuses based on patient-reported clinical outcomes. The same principle extends to hospital management, whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed, Banerjee told TechCrunch. Managers, he said, receive salaries and company-wide incentives, while marketing teams focus on bringing in patients instead of the revenue those patients generate. Moreover, every employee, including doctors and other hospital staff, receives equity in Even. The idea is to give employees a stake in the startup’s long-term performance, not to reward them for generating more medical bills.

articles.title: No agenda, no rush, no leaving San Francisco: Benchmark’s partners on investing in a frenzied market | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Benchmark may have grown its funds and swapped out some partners, but onstage the five who are left sounded like friends who just happen to be running one of the Valley’s most storied firms
articles.body_text: The players sometimes change. I sat down with four of Benchmark’s partners three years ago , and three of those individuals are no longer with the firm. The capital commitments have changed, too. This summer, Benchmark announced $2 billion across two funds, marking only the second time in its 31-year history that it has veered from raising a far smaller vehicle. But at this week’s TechCrunch Disrupt, the venture firm’s five partners convincingly portrayed a close-knit team that’s not about to put the pedal to the metal, even as many of their rivals do exactly that. The world may be speeding up, but they’re investing at the pace Benchmark always has: just two or three new bets per year per partner. The world is drowning in information, yet their Monday partner meetings still have no agenda. And while economic indicators point to trouble ahead, they don’t seem too bothered, seeing many of the warning signs as products of X-fueled hysteria. Here’s what Benchmark’s five general partners — gathered together on our stage — had to say at the show. Some of the comments below have been edited for length and clarity; you can watch the full interview at the end of the article. Benchmark has evolved in some ways, including a bigger core fund and a new growth fund. How do you think about adapting without losing what makes you Benchmark? Peter Fenton: The craft that hasn’t changed is the core fund: working closely with founders at the beginning. It’s usually a 10-to-15-year commitment, [working] shoulder to shoulder, and that doesn’t scale. There’s also been inflation. We held the core fund at $500 million for 20 years, and it has just inflated to be consistent with the existing economy, which we hadn’t done and that was probably a tactical error on our part. [As for the growth fund] it’s an expansion of our mandate. In some ways, we get permission from the ecosystem to do more than just the core early-stage business. [Not having this previously] was a fork in our eye. A number of opportunities that came to Benchmark would have returned somewhere between 10 and 1,000x to Benchmark, and we were constricted by our early-stage focus. Are you thinking to make handful of bets with that $1.25 billion growth fund? Fenton: We all have different answers, which is the beauty of a partnership. I’d love for us to have, as that great J.P. Morgan paper puts it, the agony and ecstasy of a concentrated portfolio. If the fund is successful, one or two investments will generate 90% of the returns. So I think it’s four to six, maybe seven to eight. Ev, you joined Benchmark late last year. You’ve worked at Founders Fund, Bond, and Kleiner Perkins. How does Benchmark differ? Ev Randall: Every firm is ultimately a collection of the people within the firm and how they work together. Some are very hierarchical, with a 50- or 60-person investment team and investment processes that are federated into product groups. And then you have small partnerships. Very early in my career, I was drawn to small partnerships because they allow a higher level of throughput and fidelity in your conversations, where you don’t feel like you’re making decisions through some Byzantine corporate structure. You’re going out on the field together, like a sports team. And then the other piece is: You have to find your people, You have to find people who you not only like but admire. With Benchmark, with the current crop of GPs, it was obvious that everyone liked each other and got along, but it went deeper than that. It’s a group that admires each other and learns from each other. That mix of attributes is very rare, and when I saw it, I immediately wanted to join, and I think Jack felt the same way also as a newcomer. Jack, you joined in February, but it was just a year ago that you raised a second, $275 million fund for your own firm in what you told the Wall Street Journal took one week. You have a hugely popular podcast. Why join Benchmark?

articles.title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund.
articles.body_text: Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good. Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.” There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study . But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.” Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.” If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months. articles.title: Everyone’s watching the Elizabeth Holmes documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: "You Can See Everything" is having the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film.
articles.body_text: “You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film. The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic . The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, TV shows, and other documentaries. But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing. While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight, and I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.) TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday . She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey. The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through. Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend , and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10. And Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” — hampered, perhaps, by resistance from social platforms and a four-hour runtime — made only $306,702 this weekend. articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian's next act | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
articles.body_text: As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe , I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either. Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon , a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software. Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.) Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.” So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.” Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals. And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles. “Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.” Bedrock Robotics , a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million , Axios reported, citing sources. Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing . Evos , a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures. Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.

articles.body_text: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday. Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates. Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%. Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.” One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineer compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.” In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized. Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining. The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . articles.title: X was supposed to be a bank by now
articles.summary: When he bought Twitter for $44 billion two years ago, Elon Musk said he wanted to turn the social network into an “everything app.” So far, X hasn’t achieved that vision.
articles.body_text: When Elon Musk was forced to buy Twitter two years ago, he said his goal was to turn the platform into two things: the “digital town square” and the “everything app.” He has failed at both goals. X isn’t something that is upsetting “the far right and the far left equally,” Instead, it has become Musk’s political weapon. In fact, he may be so preoccupied with trying to get Donald Trump elected that he has forgotten that X was supposed to be a bank by now. This time last year, Musk said in an internal X meeting that it “would blow my mind” if the service couldn’t handle “someone’s entire financial life” by the end of 2024. The first step toward this vision is a Venmo-like payment feature that’s still in development. X says it has secured money transmitter licenses to process payments in 38 states, including California, but has yet to get approval in key states like New York. Musk’s history of owning X has been nothing but broken promises. According to his own words, X was also supposed to be a dating service, a viable LinkedIn alternative for recruiting, and a YouTube killer by now. He said he was going to get rid of bots, too. I get more spam in my DMs than I did before Musk owned Twitter, and foreign governments have recently used bots on X to stoke division around the US presidential election. In some cases, X’s creator program means people are literally getting paid to manipulate the platform. One likely reason X has executed so poorly in the last two years is that, as long as he still has a personal megaphone, Musk may not actually care about the future of the product anymore. Network effects are strong with social networks, and X has remained surprisingly active in certain tech circles. The AI community’s obsession with it continues to amaze me given that all they’re doing is giving free training data to Musk’s AI model, Grok. His new obsession is trying to compete with OpenAI, which he helped start and then abandoned right before it struck gold with ChatGPT. He’s already raising even more money for his rival firm behind Grok, xAI, at a valuation north of $40 billion, which, on paper, would make his AI startup worth meaningfully more than X itself. He’s raising money out of necessity: I’ve heard Musk has already spent the $6 billion he raised for xAI earlier this year and needs more to buy additional compute from Nvidia, which announced this week that he plans to add another 100,000 H100s at his Colossus supercomputer site in Memphis, Tennessee. He also needs more capital to compete with the steep compensation packages top AI researchers can get elsewhere. Musk’s focus on increasing the value of xAI has to sting a bit for X employees, who were told they would be able to sell their shares every six months like SpaceX insiders can. This has yet to happen once. Company insiders I’ve spoken to doubt it ever will. After only two years, it increasingly looks like Musk thinks of X not as a town square or an everything app but as his personal Fox News and source of training data. Earnings notes A few observations from a busy week of tech earnings: * My cluster is bigger than yours: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg made a point to mention that LLama 4 is training on more than 100,000 Nvidia H100s, which just happens to be the size of Elon Musk’s xAI supercomputer. Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Amazon will collectively spend $200 billion on capital expenditures — the majority of which is going to developing AI — and have all warned that spending will go up next year. (The US government spent about $126 billion on infrastructure last year, by comparison.) When CEOs are bragging about how much compute they have, they mainly have one constituent in mind: the AI researchers they are trying to poach from their rivals. * The most expensive acquihire of all time: Google confirmed that it paid a staggering $2.7 billion to rehire Character.AI CEO Noam Shazeer, along with his cofounder and roughly 30 of their researchers. The tidbit was included in Google’s Q3 earnings paperwork under a section creatively titled “Business Combinations,” which mentions “$2.7 billion of goodwill and $413 million of intangible assets” associated with the deal. As I reported last week, Shazeer is now co-leading the Gemini team and working on a reasoning model. Despite Google entering into a “non-exclusive license” to use Character’s LLM, I’ve confirmed the Gemini team has no intention of using it. * A change in tone: It’s clear that Microsoft and OpenAI are disentangling. During Microsoft’s earnings call this week, CEO Satya Nadella mostly focused on the financial upside of the company’s investment and not its product partnership with OpenAI. OpenAI’s launch of web search in ChatGPT makes barely any mention of the fact that it’s powered by Bing. Then there’s the news that GitHub Copilot is now also offering access to Claude and Gemini. Here’s where I’ll just note that OpenAI can get out of its contract with Microsoft if it declares it has reached AGI, which Sam Altman is now saying is “achievable with current hardware.” * Still waiting for Alexa: As I reported back in March, Amazon has been working on its own foundational model to hopefully revive its Alexa line of devices. The plan was originally to have debuted this Alexa reboot by now, but Bloomberg reports that the announcement has been pushed to 2025 due to lackluster results internally. On Amazon’s earnings call this week, executives confirmed that Alexa will have its brains replaced with a new AI model “in the near future.” (Relatedly, my colleagues published a series of great stories this week looking at the last decade of the Alexa product line.) Overheard “I think Nvidia is undervalued.” – SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son is always entertaining to listen to. His recent appearance at the Future Investment Initiative forum in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, is no exception. Fresh off investing hundreds of millions of dollars in OpenAI’s latest funding round, he says that $9 trillion of capital expenditures seems “very reasonable” for achieving AGI, which he estimates will also require more than 400 gigawatts of electricity. Job board Some interesting tech career moves you may have missed lately: * Jay Parikh, the exec who built much of early Facebook’s engineering culture and more recently was CEO of Lacework, is joining Microsoft’s senior leadership team. CEO Satya Nadella says, “We will share more on his role and focus in the next few months.” * Dave Burke, Google’s ex-Android engineering chief, is now the CTO of Arc, a biomedical research nonprofit. * Peter Stern, a former deputy of Apple’s Eddy Cue and recent executive at Ford, is now the CEO of Peloton. * Rachel Whetstone, Netflix’s head of communications, and Dean Garfield, Netflix’s policy chief, are leaving as the streamer looks for a head of global affairs to oversee both functions. More links * If you haven’t already, make sure to read The Verge’s guide to next week’s presidential election, which features the only endorsement you’ll read that mentions USB-C. * Huh: Apple is acquiring the Pixelmator image editor and buying a 20 percent stake in GlobalStar, its satellite service provider for the iPhone. * There’s new evidence of rampant wash trading on Polymarket. * OSI’s official definition of open-source AI has been published. (Sorry, Meta!) * Bluesky board member Mike Masnick writes about “the state of decentralized social media.” * ByteDance founder Zhang Yiming is officially China’s richest person. * Meta published new AI research on robotics. * Claude released a native app for Mac and Windows. articles.title: How Big Tech is swallowing the AI industry
articles.summary: Amazon has replicated an antitrust-avoidance playbook pioneered by Microsoft with its hiring of most of the team behind buzzy AI startup Adept.
articles.body_text: A couple of months ago, I was sitting in the audience at a tech conference in San Fransisco watching Bloomberg’s Emily Chang interview Reid Hoffman. She asked about Microsoft’s hiring of the team behind Inflection, a would-be OpenAI competitor that Hoffman co-founded. It was an acquisition in everything but name, clearly designed to avoid the scrutiny of antitrust regulators. Not only had Microsoft (where Hoffman is a board member) hired most of Inflection’s employees — it also licensed the startup’s technology in a way that seemed designed to make its investors whole. Speaking with Chang that day onstage, Hoffman predicted that what happened to Inflection will become a “pattern” for future AI deals. We are seeing that pattern play out now. Last Friday, Amazon announced that it is hiring most of the team behind Adept, another would-be OpenAI competitor that raised about $400 million from top-tier investors to build, in the words of CEO David Luan, “a new type of giant model that turns natural language into actions on your machine.” Alexandra Miller, an Amazon spokesperson, told The Verge that the company had hired “close to” to 66 percent of Adept’s employees. In an internal memo published by GeekWire’s Taylor Soper, SVP Rohit Prasad said that, like Microsoft with Inflection, Amazon will also be licensing Adept’s technology to “accelerate our roadmap for building digital agents that can automate software workflows.” Adept’s corporate blog post about the news suggests it was running out of money: “Continuing with Adept’s initial plan of building both useful general intelligence and an enterprise agent product would’ve required spending significant attention on fundraising for our foundation models, rather than bringing to life our agent vision.” Recent reports say the company has been looking to sell itself. The reality is that building leading AI models is extremely costly, and raising $400 million isn’t even enough to compete these days. Big Tech, meanwhile, is flush with cash and looking to get in on what everyone perceives to be the next big thing. It’s logical for more AI startups to go the way of Inflection and Adept as the industry consolidates. The problem for Big Tech is that they are no longer allowed to buy companies like they once did. The current antitrust enforcement regime would most certainly try to block an Amazon acquisition of Adept, whether there is a strong legal argument for doing so or not. (Amazon execs are still seething about not being allowed to buy a robot vacuum cleaner company.) Even still, capitalism finds a way. What Microsoft did to Inflection, and what Amazon just did to Adept, is the new Big Tech playbook for swallowing the AI industry and getting away with it. Silicon Valley has a storied history of acquihires, where a startup is gutted for its people and left for dead. Microsoft and Amazon have done what are essentially reverse acquihires, where the hiring of people and a corresponding licensing deal is designed to disguise what is actually an acquisition. Reid Hoffman, meanwhile, should probably be congratulated for more than just an accurate prediction about the future of these deals — one of Adept’s earliest investors was none other than his venture capital firm, Greylock. Correction, July 1st: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated the percentage of Adept employees hired by Amazon. The percentage is “close to” 66 percent, not 80 percent.

The moral bankruptcy of Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz
articles.summary: Two of the most famous investors in Silicon Valley endorsed Donald Trump. This is less about tech generally than their investment portfolio, specifically.
articles.body_text: Last week, the founders of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz declared their allegiance to Donald Trump in their customary fashion: talking about money on a podcast. “Sorry, Mom,” Ben Horowitz says in an episode of The Ben & Marc Show. “I know you’re going to be mad at me for this. But, like, we have to do it.” Marc Andreessen and Horowitz insist they voted for Democrats until now. They are friends with liberals. They claim to be nervous about the social blowback they will receive for this, especially because of the historically progressive nature of the tech industry and the Bay Area. But given the general movement among their class toward Trump, I think those claims about being nervous are overblown, if not performative. There is, for instance, Elon Musk’s pro-Trump super PAC, which has support from Sequoia Capital’s Shaun Maguire and 8VC’s Joe Lonsdale, among other notables. (The Wall Street Journal reported Musk is planning to donate $45 million a month, which Musk has denied.) There’s the $160 million the crypto movement has put forward in support of crypto-friendly candidates. We can’t forget their VC pal David Sacks speaking at the Republican National Convention. And last but not least, there’s Trump’s running mate choice of JD Vance, a former venture capitalist whose firm’s investors included Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt, and Andreessen himself. This isn’t a movement. It’s a clique. The podcast itself is an extraordinary performance. At one point, Andreessen concedes that their major problems with President Joe Biden — the ones that led them to support Trump — are what most voters would consider “subsidiary” issues. “It doesn’t have anything to do with the big issues that people care about,” he says. If we take this podcast at face value, we are to believe that these subsidiary issues are the only reason they’ve chosen to endorse and donate to Trump. These subsidiary issues take precedence for Andreessen and Horowitz over, say, mass deportations and Project 2025’s attempt to end no-fault divorce. We are looking at a simple trade against personal liberty — abortion, the rights of gay and trans people, and possibly democracy itself — in favor of crypto, AI, and a tax policy they like better. For Horowitz, “probably the most emotional topic” is crypto — a16z started a $4.5 billion crypto fund in 2022, and the pair believe that the Biden administration has been deeply unfair to crypto. In Horowitz’s view, the Biden administration “basically subverted the rule of law to attack the crypto industry.” Certainly much of the crypto industry prefers Trump. But it seems obvious that there has been a lot of intra-agency squabbling as Congress dithered on passing any laws. To place the blame squarely on Biden is bizarre, particularly when we have Trump’s chaotic previous term as guidance. Sure, Trump is no longer saying Bitcoin is “a scam against the dollar,” as he did in 2021; he is scheduled to speak at the Bitcoin conference this year. But his record in office is not exactly pro-crypto. During the Trump administration, financial regulator FinCEN initially asked the public to provide comments on a crypto rule change over a 15-day period that included Christmas Eve, Christmas Day, New Year’s Eve, and New Year’s Day, which effectively shortened the comment window by four working days. There is also the Ripple Labs enforcement case, in which the SEC is seeking a $1.95 billion fine; it, too, dates to the Trump administration. The pair’s complaints about Gary Gensler, the current head of the Securities and Exchange Commission, are striking. They are particularly annoyed that he won’t pay attention to them. “We’re the largest crypto investors or largest blockchain investors in the world, and we’ve requested meetings with him at least a half a dozen times,” Horowitz says. Gensler has not met with them. Neither, they say, has Senator Elizabeth Warren or Biden himself. In fact, Andreessen makes it clear that he expects presidential attention, something he’s been getting since he was 23. Given the number of times Andreessen and Horowitz make references to various meetings with various politicians, it’s easy to get the impression that they are mostly insulted that they are being treated like ordinary constituents. From crypto, we move to AI, which Andreessen and Horowitz don’t think is being regulated correctly either. According to Horowitz, AI is as powerful as, or more powerful than, the internet and the global computer industry from the 1950s on. “This may be the biggest technological boom of all time,” Andreessen says. Andreessen says in his newsletter-cum-manifesto, “The Little Tech Agenda,” that he is worried that AI will face similar scrutiny to crypto. The FTC has issued guidance to the AI industry that indicated it will pursue companies that exaggerate what their AI can do, say they are using AI when they are not, and recklessly put products on the market without properly analyzing the risks. Meanwhile, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has told lenders that they must supply a reason for a credit denial that’s better than just “computer says no” when using AI models. These regulations have little to do with technology and a lot to do with old-fashioned lying. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz single out Biden’s executive order about artificial intelligence. The order requires companies to disclose the presence of very large models, as well as to provide the government information about what the plans are for the model, what cybersecurity measures are taken to protect those models, and the results of red-team testing for sensitive subjects, among other things. This is in keeping with Horowitz’s assertion about the seriousness of the technology. So what’s the problem? The two focus on computing power. The disclosure requirements apply to “any model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 1026 integer or floating-point operations, or using primarily biological sequence data and using a quantity of computing power greater than 1023 integer or floating-point operations.” Andreessen and Horowitz think specifying such a limit is ridiculous. Little tech “will be snuffed out by this kind of regulation,” Horowitz says. It is perhaps worth noting that nothing above the size specified in the executive order — the size Andreessen and Horowitz object to — even exists yet, according to Arati Prabhakar, Biden’s top tech advisor. The fundamental complaint here is that these two believe that the Biden administration’s approach to AI “enshrine[s] the two or three companies that they believe are the only companies that matter as sort of permanent monopolies,” Andreessen says. “And they’re going to just basically destroy the startup ecosystem underneath that.” Andreessen Horowitz is, of course, invested in that ecosystem, having earmarked $2.25 billion for AI applications and infrastructure. The anti-monopoly rhetoric is in keeping with a16z’s latest marketing push. According to Andreessen’s newsletter, startups are threatened by the government, which is “now far more hostile to new startups than it used to be.” Besides his objections to the way the SEC has increased its oversight of crypto, he is also upset that a stepped-up interest in antitrust has made it more difficult for him to exit investments. “Regulatory agencies are punitively blocking startups from being acquired by the same big companies the government is preferencing in so many other ways,” Andreessen writes. After all, the Federal Trade Commission has launched an inquiry into Big Tech’s partnerships and investments with startups — with the goal of seeing if those partnerships squash competition. The irony is so obvious it’s almost embarrassing to point it out. Andreessen says he is upset that Big Tech is too powerful, but he opposes antitrust action because that blocks a route for VCs to exit. Either you’re comfortable with Big Tech getting bigger, in which case acquisitions are fine, or you want little tech to be competitive, which means blocking industry consolidation. Mainly, it seems that Andreessen believes in cashing out. In the podcast, Andreessen and Horowitz pointedly name Google as a threat to startups. “Google, I think we would all agree, is more powerful than probably 95 percent of countries in the world,” Horowitz says at one point. Google, specifically, is a sore spot with the right wing. Vice presidential nominee Vance has already said it should be broken up. Vance believes Google is controlling information and skewing too far left. Of course, Google’s moderation policies don’t just apply to Google News — they also affect YouTube, which hosts a great many right-wing podcasts without issue. It’s unclear how seriously to take Andreessen and Horowitz’s complaints about Big Tech because the complaints don’t quite square with their behavior. For instance, Facebook is similarly powerful and influential, especially in AI. Andreessen sits on its board. A16z is invested in OpenAI, which has a partnership with Microsoft — and both have lobbied strenuously for more regulation around AI. It sure seems like if a16z wants to change things at those big companies, someone could simply pick up the phone. At this point in the podcast, you could squint and say maybe the concern about AI and crypto is really about technology and progress. But from those two topics, we move on to classic rich guy shit of the most tedious kind: tax reform. Andreessen says it was “the final straw for me. This is the thing that tipped me hard.” They are upset about a proposal to alter capital gains taxes. Capital gains are paid on investment assets, and they are typically paid when the investment is sold and the gains are, in industry terms, “realized.” The new Biden treasury proposal means that for people whose wealth is worth more than $100 million, any unrealized capital gains will be taxed, too. This is what has Andreessen and Horowitz in a tizzy. It means that if they own a clutch of highly valued startup shares, they will have to pay taxes on them before they cash out. This is a “very scary proposal,” Horowitz says. Startups are illiquid assets, Andreessen points out. “Startups never go up and down. They’re never overvalued,” says Horowtiz, dryly. “There’s no bubbles.” Andreessen notes that the way the value of a startup is calculated for the purposes of this proposed tax has to do with the latest round’s valuation. Historically, one of the ways that Andreessen Horowitz has approached startup investing is to inflate a company’s valuation; it is “the OG when it comes to doling out speculative startup valuations.” The new proposed tax punishes this kind of behavior — a high valuation means a high tax. “This makes startups completely implausible,” says Andreessen. “Venture capital just ends. Firms like ours don’t exist.” This is followed by an anxiety spiral that is sort of difficult to convey in text; I suggest you listen for yourself. “California is done,” says Andreessen. “It’s total destruction.” The taxes won’t just target the wealthy; they’ll come for everyone. “Once the structure gets established, the politicians do what they do: they’ll walk the numbers up,” Andreessen says. “Presto chango, we’re Argentina!” says Horowitz. Finally, Horowitz gets ahold of himself. “By the way, this one probably won’t get all the way through the system,” he says. “But it might!” There is another issue that might cause wreckage throughout Silicon Valley. It is immigration. An awful lot of immigrants comprise Silicon Valley’s talent pool — a huge swath of engineers in the US are on H-1B visas. The Trump / Vance ticket is virulently anti-immigrant. The current CEOs of Google, Microsoft, Adobe, and IBM are all immigrants. So are Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg and Bill Gates are involved in Fwd.us, a lobbying group dedicated to immigration reform that Musk and Sacks both left. If there were an issue that would rally the people who care most about progress, innovation, and talent, you’d think protecting the immigrants who’ve built lives and careers in tech would be it. Stopping immigration is a core issue of the Trump campaign. During the Republican National Convention, delegates held up signs saying “Mass Deportation Now.” Trump has called the H-1B, the visa many tech workers use to come to Silicon Valley, “very bad” and “unfair” to US workers. In his previous term, he targeted H-1B visa applications specifically; in the fiscal year 2018, almost 25 percent of applications were denied, up from about 13 percent the year before. In fiscal year 2019, 20 percent of H-1B applications were denied. The denials plummeted after several Trump administration rules were thrown out by courts; the denial rate in 2022 was just 2 percent. Immigration plainly matters for crypto — as Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin says, “The crypto industry is uniquely international, and so immigration law is crypto law.” Buterin is one of the most influential voices in crypto, and Ethereum is the foundation for a swath of Andreessen Horowitz’s investment portfolio. Among the investments that rely on it are MakerDAO, VeeFriends, Dapper Labs, and EigenLayer. It is remarkable that the founder of Ethereum is saying that voting for Trump is against the crypto ethos, and the big crypto investors are doing it anyway. The word “immigration” is only mentioned by Andreessen and Horowitz in the podcast when they discuss the rally in which someone attempted an assassination: Trump had turned his head to look at a chart that purported to show illegal immigration into the US as the bullet whizzed by. I wondered why such an important issue for tech wasn’t addressed, so I emailed Margit Wennmachers, a16z’s PR guru, to ask. She didn’t reply. After I finished listening to the podcast, a few things kept nagging at me. Take the very beginning of the podcast. Once upon a time, Andreessen says, you could get very rich and then give the money away in philanthropy, “and you get enormous credit for that. And, you know, it absolves you of whatever.” At some point in the last 10 years, some people suggested that maybe rich people should pay more taxes instead of giving their money away — that perhaps the whims of some random rich person are not the best way to support the most vulnerable in our society. Andreessen and Horowitz suggest that this critique of philanthropy is simply jealousy. It also unbalanced “the deal.” “The deal,” as described on the podcast, is vague. To my ear, it sounds like this: Tech companies could basically do whatever they wanted, as long as people who worked there paid high taxes and donated enough money to charitable causes. The money — taxes, donations — made them the good guys. Andreessen and Horowitz point to the mid-2010s — that is, the era of low interest rates — as the time of “the deal” unraveling. Notably, this is around the time that the tech hype cycle became obvious even to people who weren’t paying attention. This year, it’s scooters! Now it’s viral media companies! Now it’s metaverse! Now it’s crypto! Now it’s AI! These ideas were more or less rejected by the market, except possibly AI. The one thing all these hype cycles had in common was VCs talking their books, as publicly as possible. That charge was led by Andreessen Horowitz. So now, instead of investing in things the market wants, Andreessen and Horowitz appear to be gambling on legislation instead. Their timing is remarkable; not even a week after their Trump endorsement, Biden dropped out of the race, rallying the Democrats behind Vice President Kamala Harris. In the hours immediately following the announcement, small-money donors raised $46.7 million for her campaign. By endorsing Trump, Andreessen and Horowitz have effectively lost whatever leverage they might have had with the Harris campaign. But maybe that doesn’t matter. Near the end of the podcast, Horowitz says that he was shaken by the assassination attempt on Donald Trump because he’s friends with Ivanka, his daughter, and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law. “Ivanka and the kids were just at my house,” Horowitz says, of learning Trump was shot. “We went to see David Copperfield and all that. So my brain was almost frozen because I had this feeling about, ‘Oh my god, Grandpa just got shot.’” As for Andreessen, he has been inveighing against “woke” capital, engaging in Twitter culture wars, and complaining about what he views as the media’s hostility to free speech for a while now. In Andreessen’s 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” he lists what he terms “patron saints” of the movement. They include Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, an Italian futurist who was also the co-author of The Fascist Manifesto; Nick Land, whose writing is a foundational text for the so-called alt-right; Neven Sesardic, a philosopher who argues that race is biologically real and not socially constructed; and Vilfredo Pareto, who argued that democracy is an illusion. And this talk about democracy brings me to Curtis Yarvin, personal friend of vice presidential candidate Vance. Yarvin, a software developer, is openly anti-democracy. (Yarvin’s recent newsletter, in response to Biden dropping out, enthusiastically advocates for a return to monarchy. Freak shit.) One of Yarvin’s ideas, called “retire all government employees” or RAGE, is part of Project 2025, a Heritage Foundation proposal for what Trump should do if he wins. This rhetoric was echoed by Vance in 2021, who called out Yarvin by name. So this VC cabal is trading against the basic principles of America — not merely against personal freedom, but democracy itself — in the hopes of profit. It’s not the first time tech has made the trade against freedom; IBM made it during the Holocaust. In venture capital, you are what you fund. Andreessen and Horowitz understand this, even embody it. But they aren’t just funding the issues they discuss on their podcast; they are funding Trump and Vance. That means those donations are anti-abortion, anti-immigration, and possibly even anti-democracy because that is what the Trump / Vance ticket stands for. These are not subsidiary issues: these are now what two of Silicon Valley’s most prominent figures now stand for, too. Is that a good investment? Correction July 24: An earlier version of this article misstated the donation strategy of a crypto super PAC. The group also spends money on Democratic candidates, not just right-wing ones.

It was an acquisition in everything but name, clearly designed to avoid the scrutiny of antitrust regulators. Not only had Microsoft (where Hoffman is a board member) hired most of Inflection’s employees — it also licensed the startup’s technology in a way that seemed designed to make its investors whole. Speaking with Chang that day onstage, Hoffman predicted that what happened to Inflection will become a “pattern” for future AI deals. We are seeing that pattern play out now. Last Friday, Amazon announced that it is hiring most of the team behind Adept, another would-be OpenAI competitor that raised about $400 million from top-tier investors to build, in the words of CEO David Luan, “a new type of giant model that turns natural language into actions on your machine.” Alexandra Miller, an Amazon spokesperson, told The Verge that the company had hired “close to” to 66 percent of Adept’s employees. In an internal memo published by GeekWire’s Taylor Soper, SVP Rohit Prasad said that, like Microsoft with Inflection, Amazon will also be licensing Adept’s technology to “accelerate our roadmap for building digital agents that can automate software workflows.” Adept’s corporate blog post about the news suggests it was running out of money: “Continuing with Adept’s initial plan of building both useful general intelligence and an enterprise agent product would’ve required spending significant attention on fundraising for our foundation models, rather than bringing to life our agent vision.” Recent reports say the company has been looking to sell itself. The reality is that building leading AI models is extremely costly, and raising $400 million isn’t even enough to compete these days. Big Tech, meanwhile, is flush with cash and looking to get in on what everyone perceives to be the next big thing. It’s logical for more AI startups to go the way of Inflection and Adept as the industry consolidates. The problem for Big Tech is that they are no longer allowed to buy companies like they once did. The current antitrust enforcement regime would most certainly try to block an Amazon acquisition of Adept, whether there is a strong legal argument for doing so or not. (Amazon execs are still seething about not being allowed to buy a robot vacuum cleaner company.) Even still, capitalism finds a way. What Microsoft did to Inflection, and what Amazon just did to Adept, is the new Big Tech playbook for swallowing the AI industry and getting away with it. Silicon Valley has a storied history of acquihires, where a startup is gutted for its people and left for dead. Microsoft and Amazon have done what are essentially reverse acquihires, where the hiring of people and a corresponding licensing deal is designed to disguise what is actually an acquisition. Reid Hoffman, meanwhile, should probably be congratulated for more than just an accurate prediction about the future of these deals — one of Adept’s earliest investors was none other than his venture capital firm, Greylock. Correction, July 1st: A previous version of this story incorrectly stated the percentage of Adept employees hired by Amazon. The percentage is “close to” 66 percent, not 80 percent.

articles.body_text: C-ledaren Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist har fått talmannens sonderingsuppdrag. Hon hoppas på en regering med C, S, MP, L och KD, erfar Expressen. – Min ambition är att bidra till en lösning på regeringsfrågan, säger hon själv. Samtliga partier har tackat ja till möte med C-ledaren. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. På måndagen stod det klart att Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist får sondera för en ny regering. Hon får till på måndag på sig. Hennes uppgift är inte i första hand att själv bli statsminister, utan att utröna om det mittenalternativ som C vill se är möjligt. – Jag är ödmjuk inför att ha fått talmannens uppdrag, sa hon i en kommentar efter beskedet. Källor i flera av de rödgröna partierna har tidigare uttryckt frustration över att Magdalena Andersson (S) arbetade för långsamt när hon hade sonderingsuppdraget. Det är en bild som också funnits inom C, och som kan ligga bakom att Thand Ringqvist direkt efter att hon fick uppgiften genast började boka in möten. Hon ska samtala med alla, även V och SD. articles.title: Polisens larm innan mordet: Finns risk för hämnddåd
articles.summary: Det fanns en aktiv hotbild mot familjen vars 24-åriga dotter mördades i Älvsjö – kopplad till en nära släkting.
articles.body_text: Det fanns en hotbild mot familjen vars 24-åriga dotter mördades i Älvsjö i helgen. Hotbilden kopplas till en nära släkting som friats i dubbla rättegångar – för mord och mordförsök. ”Förlåt mig”, skrev släktingen i ett brev från häktet till sin familj. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Två tonårspojkar är misstänkta för dödsskjutningen av en 24-årig kvinna i Älvsjö under en idrottsturnering i fredags. Ytterligare en pojke eftersöks av polis, rapporterar TV4 Nyheterna . Han ska ha setts på övervakningsfilm från en ”tryckarlägenhet” – en lägenhet man har som bas vid ett planerat mord. Även de två misstänkta pojkarna ska ha varit där. Åklagare Lukas Tigerstrand har meddelat att han ser goda chanser att mordet blir uppklarat. Åklagare har sagt att man tittar på olika motiv. Något man tittar på är den dokumenterade hotbild som funnits mot kvinnans familj, genom en släkting till henne. Den 24-åriga kvinnans släkting är välkänd av polis och har dokumenterade band till kriminella nätverk i Älvsjö. Utöver mord- och mordförsöksmisstankar de senaste åren har han suttit frihetsberövad flera gånger för narkotika- och vapenbrott. Enligt dokumentation hos polisen har han varit ”drivande” i att vilja ta tillbaka området och hämnas tidigare situationer. Enligt polisens uppgifter har släktingen samarbetat med kriminella nätverk i södra Stockholm, och rekryterat yngre. Han åtalades – men frikändes – för inblandning i ett mord 2022. Förra året frikändes han igen för mordförsök på två män.
